extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and working authors seeking a literary/booking agent
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for authors to select (and reassess) a literary agent who will represent their work and manage the business side of their writing career. Covers reputation, communication style, genre fit, career-stage fit, ethics, and practical due diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Your agent works for you
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an offer of representation is made, the power dynamic inverts — the agent works for the author and the author should choose them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the relationship as a choice: you should be deliberate about who you accept, because the agent will act as your business partner and represent your interests. Don't accept any agent just because you can get representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term business-partner fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about who will be the right business partner over the course of your career — ideally an author-agent relationship will last years or decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the agent can help you 'run your business,' how they will carry part of your authorial brand, and whether their operating style will support your long-term goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence / ability to do the job
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't choose someone who is bad at their job; a poor agent can actively hold you back (e.g., sit on your manuscript or sell incompetently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning flags (e.g., long delays, lack of activity) are serious because a bad sale attempt can make later sales difficult. Prioritize demonstrable competence and results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation with editors and industry
rubrics_metrics.description: An agent's reputation and way of operating will influence how editors/publishers perceive you during initial contacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the agent has a reputation (good or bad) that could color meetings and pitches; good taste and professional habits matter because they reflect on you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' recommendations / client satisfaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask to speak with the agent's other authors; if the agent's clients are unwilling to recommend them, that's a red flag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct referrals and testimonials from current/past clients are strong signals. If authors happily recommend their agent, that is a positive sign; lack of willingness to recommend suggests caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due diligence: check online resources and network
rubrics_metrics.description: Use online tools and personal networks to check an agent's reputation and for red flags (e.g., QueryTracker, Absolute Write, Publisher's Weekly, Locus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search the agent's name with terms like 'scam' or 'harassment' for scandals; talk to writers in your network; consult sale listings and trade publications to verify track record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre coverage / market fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the agent work in the genres and markets you want to play in (including the ability to represent cross-genre work)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agent who covers the genres you want to write (or who is willing to go with you as you hop genres) is valuable. Ask about their experience selling in your target markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of editorial involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Different agents offer different levels of hands-on editorial support; know whether you want an agent who edits aggressively or who is hands-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the agent and their authors about how editorial they are. Match the agent’s editorial style to your needs (developmental help vs. minimal editing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication style and frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Alignment on how the agent communicates (formal vs. casual) and how often you expect contact is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify expectations (weekly, monthly, quarterly contact). Discuss preferred formats (emails, phone calls) and ensure compatibility — communication mismatch can cause friction even with a competent agent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity / fills your weak spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose someone who complements you professionally — someone who fills in your weaknesses rather than duplicates your strengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify what you lack (e.g., aggressive negotiation, relationship-building) and prefer an agent who provides those skills. Mary Robinette's choice favored someone who was a 'shark' to balance her strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career-stage fit / appropriate aggression
rubrics_metrics.description: Your needs change over time; consider whether an agent's aggressiveness and strategy match your current career stage and sales trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may need a more aggressive agent at certain points, or a different approach if sales decline or opportunities change. Be open to changing agents as your career evolves; weigh costs and benefits of switching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and fiduciary behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The agent must act in your best interests and not against their writers; moral behavior and honest dealings matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for publicized incidents of agents acting against writers' interests. Seek a 'moral agent' (alignment on ethics, money, and professional behavior) and avoid agents with ethical red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to answer questions / do due diligence together
rubrics_metrics.description: A good agent expects and welcomes questions; the candidate author should actively vet the relationship and ask detailed questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time talking through expectations (Mary & Dongwon spent many hours on the phone). If a prospective client isn't asking questions, agents may worry — be proactive in learning how the relationship will work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical track record and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the agent's measurable results: sales, deals, and who they have sold to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trade publications and sales listings to confirm the agent's ability to deliver favorable results (e.g., better advances, advantageous terms). Anecdotes of concrete wins (like getting a raise on a deal) are informative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal chemistry but not a substitute for competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal rapport ('charisma') matters for ease of working together, but charisma is 'not a dump stat' — it cannot replace professional competence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek someone you can connect with, but prioritize job performance first. Communication and manners matter, yet the agent must be competent at representing you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect agent evolution and maintain open communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents' careers and circumstances change; keep lines of communication open and revisit goals regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss goals periodically to ensure needs are being met; changes in the agent's workload or role at an agency can affect the relationship and may prompt reassessment.
